newsitem.title: USA: House passes $92 billion bill for 17 agencies.
newsitem.headline: House passes $92 billion bill for 17 agencies.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives on Wednesday passed a $91.7 billion spending bill for next year's programmes for veterans, housing, environmental protection, science and space.

The bill, which passed 397-31, more narrowly survived an effort by Democrats to send it back to a House Committee to beef up spending for veterans, the homeless and to reclaim dangerously polluted urban sites.
The bill, which funds 17 agencies, could draw the White House's ire because it slashes the AmeriCorps programme for volunteer community service, one of President Bill Clinton's prized programmes.

The White House said it would object if the final legislation emerged from Congress without the $400 million AmeriCorps programme largely intact. Lawmakers were expected to restore the funds when the House and Senate mesh their bills.
Nearly half of the bill's spending -- $40.4 billion -- goes to Veterans Department programmes for health, housing, education and benefits.
The bill also would provide $25.1 billion for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, up $8.8 billion from last year and $550 million above the White House request.

It provides $7.2 billion for the Environmental Protection Agency, up $433 million from this year's, but $432.4 million below the president's request. The White House complained the bill did not adequately fund the Superfund hazardous waste cleanup programme, which violated the balanced budget deal.
The bill also provides $13.6 billion for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and $1.1 billion for the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
The House moved late Tuesday on a voice vote to slash the AmeriCorps programme in half, and shift $25 million from it to research on illnesses linked to the Gulf War.

Republicans long have targeted AmeriCorps, saying the programme that offers stipends towards college tuitions in effect pays each volunteer about $19,000. They say that contradicts the concept of a volunteer programme.
But Democrats say the programme provides valuable community services, as well as offering people a leg-up on a college education.

California Republican Jerry Lewis, chairman of the key appropriations subcommittee on the bill, said he expected the Americorps programme will be restored when the House and Senate bills are meshed, in order to get the president's signature.
The Senate also voted to drop $60 million that was in the bill for the first phase of building a wind simulation centre in Idaho. That money was shifted to veterans' medical care.
Opponents of stricter new air quality standards withdrew a rider that would have barred the Environmental Protection Agency from enforcing the new standards.
A group of mostly Midwestern and Ohio Valley lawmakers, who blasted the new standards as damaging to the economy and job growth, said they will push another bill to try to block the standards.

A measure to freeze funds for a programme that gives grants, loans and technical assistance to community development financial institutions also was withdrawn after long wrangling that produced a deal to make the House-Senate conference take into account that the programme was under investigation by the Treasury Department.
